cate-tuia-pe-metru-liniar: One of the first questions in any hedge project is how many plants you need. The answer depends on the species, the height of the plants at planting and how quickly you want the hedge to become dense. Below you will find the recommended spacing for the most widely used hedge plants and a calculator that quickly shows how many plants your hedge length requires.
Calculator: how many plants for your hedge
How many Thuja Smaragd per linear metre

For [Thuja Smaragd](/products/tuia-smaragd) the standard recommendation is 2–3 plants per linear metre, i.e. 35–50 cm between plants, measured trunk to trunk. Thuja Smaragd has a narrow columnar shape – at maturity it reaches 1–1.5 m in width – so if planted further apart it leaves gaps between plants for several years.
Small plants (60–100 cm): 3 plants per linear metre, for a dense hedge sooner.
Medium plants (100–150 cm): 2–3 plants per linear metre.
Large plants (over 150 cm): usually 2 plants per linear metre, as they are already wider.
Very dense planting (4 or more plants per metre) is not recommended: the plants compete for water and light, and the lower part of the hedge can become bare over time.

[Leyland cypress](/products/chiparos-leyland) grows much faster and wider than thuja, so it is planted further apart. Slow-growing species used for low clipped hedges, such as [yew](/products/tisa-taxus-baccata) and [Lonicera nitida](/products/lonicera-nitida), are planted closer together.

For most hedges a single row is enough. A double row, with plants staggered in a zig-zag, is used when you want a very dense screen from the start, a wider hedge or a better barrier against wind and noise. In this case the rows are 30–50 cm apart, and within each row the plants are spaced a little further apart than in a single row – usually 1.5–2 plants per linear metre in each row.
How to plant a hedge correctly
Mark the line of the hedge with a string and dig either individual holes or a continuous trench about 40–50 cm wide.
The hole should be at least twice as wide as the root ball or pot, and the plant is set at the same depth at which it grew.
For plants with a root ball in netting or hessian, open the material at the top but do not break up the root ball.
Backfill with soil mixed with compost, firm gently and water thoroughly straight after planting.
Cover the soil with mulch (for example pine bark) to retain moisture and reduce weeds.
In the first two years the most important job is regular watering. Most problems with newly planted hedges – yellowing or browning plants – are caused by lack of water.

For projects with hundreds or thousands of plants, it is important that the plants come from batches that are uniform in height and density, so the hedge looks even from day one. Send us the hedge length, species and desired height via the [contact](/contact) page and we will calculate the quantity and send you a quote.

cate-tuia-pe-metru-liniar.q: How many thuja do I need for 10 metres of hedge?
cate-tuia-pe-metru-liniar.a: For Thuja Smaragd, at 2–3 plants per linear metre, you need 20–30 plants for 10 metres, depending on the height of the plants.

cate-tuia-pe-metru-liniar.q: How far from a fence or building should thuja be planted?
cate-tuia-pe-metru-liniar.a: At least 40–50 cm from an existing fence or wall is recommended, so the plants have room to grow and can be trimmed on both sides.

cate-tuia-pe-metru-liniar.q: Can I plant thuja further apart to save money?
cate-tuia-pe-metru-liniar.a: You can, but the hedge will have gaps for several years. Thuja Smaragd grows slowly in width, so spacing of more than 50 cm considerably delays the hedge closing up.

cele-mai-bune-plante-pentru-gard-viu: There is no single 'best' hedge plant. The choice depends on the available space, sun exposure, the desired height, how quickly you need privacy and how much time you can spend on maintenance. Below we compare the hedge plants most widely used in residential, commercial and public projects.
The values are indicative and depend on soil, climate and care, but they show the differences between species well.
Thuja Smaragd – the classic, narrow, neat hedge

[Thuja Smaragd](/products/tuia-smaragd) is the most popular hedge plant in Romania. It takes up little width, keeps its emerald-green colour in winter and does not need frequent trimming. Its main drawbacks are sensitivity to drought in the first years and slower growth. It is the right choice for private gardens, residential developments and places where the hedge must be narrow.
Cherry laurel – dense, fast and shade-tolerant

[Cherry laurel](/products/laurocerasus-prunus-laurocerasus) has large, glossy leaves and quickly forms a dense visual and noise screen. It tolerates shade better than almost any other hedge plant, so it is very good in courtyards and between buildings. However, it takes up more width and needs trimming once or twice a year. For a detailed comparison, see [Cherry laurel or thuja](/ghiduri/laurocerasus-sau-tuia).
Photinia Red Robin – a hedge with colour

[Photinia Red Robin](/products/photinia-red-robin) produces bright red shoots in spring and after every trim. It is used on its own or combined with cherry laurel for hedges with colour accents at offices, commercial sites and residential developments. It prefers sunny sites and well-drained soils and is hardy to about -15°C.
Leyland cypress – the fastest tall hedge

If you need a tall hedge in a short time, [Leyland cypress](/products/chiparos-leyland) is hard to beat: it grows 60–100 cm per year. It suits windbreaks and screens around large properties, warehouses or industrial zones. It must be trimmed regularly, 2–3 times a year, because it does not regrow if cut back into old wood.
Yew – for clipped hedges and shade

[Yew](/products/tisa-taxus-baccata) grows slowly but is very long-lived, tolerates shade and can be clipped into precise shapes. It is preferred in formal gardens and premium landscaping. All parts of the plant are toxic, so it is not recommended next to playgrounds.
Lonicera nitida – low borders, an alternative to box

For low hedges and borders, [Lonicera nitida](/products/lonicera-nitida) is one of the best alternatives to box, which is affected by the box tree moth. It tolerates repeated trimming very well and grows quickly.
Narrow space, neat look, minimal maintenance: Thuja Smaragd.
Shade, courtyards, noise screen: cherry laurel.
Tall hedge, very fast: Leyland cypress.
Colour and decorative accents: Photinia Red Robin.
Low borders, formal gardens: Lonicera nitida or yew.

cele-mai-bune-plante-pentru-gard-viu.q: What is the best hedge plant for shade?
cele-mai-bune-plante-pentru-gard-viu.a: Cherry laurel and yew are the most suitable for shade; Thuja Smaragd and Leyland prefer sun or partial shade.

cele-mai-bune-plante-pentru-gard-viu.q: Which hedge stays green in winter?
cele-mai-bune-plante-pentru-gard-viu.a: All the plants in the table are evergreen and stay green in winter: thuja, cherry laurel, Photinia, Leyland, yew and Lonicera nitida.

gard-viu-cu-crestere-rapida: When you move into a new house, build a residential development or need to screen an industrial site, privacy matters quickly. Some hedge plants grow three to four times faster than others. Here are the fastest ones and the trade-offs of each.

[Leyland cypress](/products/chiparos-leyland) is the fastest conifer for tall hedges. In just a few years it can form a green wall 3–4 m high. Plant 1.5–2 plants per linear metre. The trade-off: it must be trimmed 2–3 times a year from the very first year, and if it is left to grow unchecked and then cut back hard, it will not regrow from old wood.

[Cherry laurel](/products/laurocerasus-prunus-laurocerasus) combines fast growth with shade tolerance and dense evergreen foliage. It is the right choice when you need a dense visual and noise screen of 1.5–3 m in gardens, car parks or residential developments.
3. Photinia Red Robin – 30–40 cm per year

[Photinia Red Robin](/products/photinia-red-robin) grows quickly and offers a bonus: the new shoots are bright red. Every trim triggers a new 'red flush'. It prefers sunny sites and well-drained soils.
4. Bamboo – an exotic, very fast screen

[Bamboo](/products/bambus) quickly creates dense screens, especially in planters on terraces and roofs. Pay attention to the type: running species spread and must be planted with a rhizome barrier, while clumping species do not spread.

If you do not need a clipped hedge but a natural, flowering screen, [lilac](/products/liliac-syringa-vulgaris) grows quickly, is extremely frost-hardy and fills the garden with fragrance in April–May. However, it loses its leaves in winter, so it does not give year-round privacy.
How to speed things up: larger plants from the start

The surest way to get instant privacy is not just the species but the height of the plants at planting. A hedge planted with 1.8–2 m plants gives privacy from day one, even with a moderately growing species such as [Thuja Smaragd](/products/tuia-smaragd). For large projects, combining larger plants at planting with a fast-growing species gives the best results.
Planting very densely 'so it closes up faster' – the plants compete with each other and become bare at the base.
Skipping trimming in the first years – fast-growing hedges must be shaped from the start, otherwise they become sparse at the base.
Neglecting watering – fast growth also means high water consumption.
All the plants above are available wholesale in several heights. See the [wholesale hedge plants](/gard-viu-en-gros) category or [request a quote](/contact) with the hedge length and desired height.

gard-viu-cu-crestere-rapida.q: What is the fastest evergreen hedge?
gard-viu-cu-crestere-rapida.a: Leyland cypress, which grows 60–100 cm per year, followed by cherry laurel and Photinia Red Robin.

gard-viu-cu-crestere-rapida.q: How long does it take for a hedge to close up?
gard-viu-cu-crestere-rapida.a: It depends on the species and plant size at planting: with Leyland or cherry laurel usually 2–3 years; with large plants at planting the effect can be almost immediate.

cand-se-planteaza-tuia-si-coniferele: Why autumn is the best time for conifers

In autumn the soil is still warm from summer while air temperatures drop. Roots keep growing while the top of the plant uses little water. Autumn rain reduces the need for watering, and the following spring the plant starts off already rooted. That is why autumn (September–November) is the preferred time for balled [conifers](/conifere-en-gros) such as [Thuja Smaragd](/products/tuia-smaragd), [blue spruce](/products/molid-albastru-picea-pungens-glauca) or [black pine](/products/pin-negru-pinus-nigra).

Spring (March–April) is the second very good period, especially for more frost-sensitive species, which need a full season to root before their first winter. The drawback is that summer follows quickly, so watering must start immediately and be kept up regularly.

Container plants can also be planted in summer, because their roots are not disturbed at planting. The condition is generous watering – daily in the first weeks during heatwaves – and planting in the morning or evening. Balled plants are not recommended in summer.
During heatwaves above 30°C without the possibility of watering.
In waterlogged soil after heavy rain – wait a few days.

cand-se-planteaza-tuia-si-coniferele.q: When is the best time to plant thuja?
cand-se-planteaza-tuia-si-coniferele.a: In autumn, September–November, or in spring, March–April. Container thuja can be planted from spring to autumn with regular watering.

cand-se-planteaza-tuia-si-coniferele.q: Can thuja be planted in winter?
cand-se-planteaza-tuia-si-coniferele.a: Only on frost-free days, in unfrozen soil. In general, autumn and spring are much safer.

plante-cu-balot-sau-in-container: Ornamental plants are mainly supplied in two forms: root-balled (the roots in a ball of soil wrapped in hessian or netting) and container-grown (in a plastic pot). Each option has clear advantages, and the right choice can lower project costs and the risk of losses.

plante-cu-balot-sau-in-container.alt: Balled conifers wrapped in netting, ready for delivery

plante-cu-balot-sau-in-container: Root-balled plants are grown in the field, directly in the soil, and lifted with a ball of soil around the roots. This is the classic form for trees, large conifers and large hedge plants.
Advantages: usually a better price for large sizes, well-developed plants, root system formed in natural soil.
Drawbacks: planted only during the dormant season (autumn and spring), the root ball is heavy, and plants must be planted as soon as possible after delivery.

Container plants are grown in pots and their roots stay intact at planting. They are the preferred form for shrubs, perennials, small and medium hedge plants, and for planting outside the classic season.

plante-cu-balot-sau-in-container.alt: Leyland cypress in containers (pots), ready for planting

plante-cu-balot-sau-in-container: Advantages: can be planted almost all year round, very good establishment, easier transport and storage.
Drawbacks: higher price for the same size, and in plants kept too long in the pot the roots can start to circle.

plante-cu-balot-sau-in-container: How to handle and plant root-balled plants
Always lift plants by the root ball, not by the trunk – otherwise the ball can come away from the roots.
If not planted immediately, keep the root balls in the shade, close together, and water them so they do not dry out.
Hessian can be left in the hole, opened at the top; wire or synthetic netting is cut and partly removed.
Set the root ball at the same depth at which the plant grew, then water thoroughly.
Large trees are anchored with stakes so the wind does not move the root ball in the first years.

plante-cu-balot-sau-in-container.alt: Balled ornamental trees on a truck for transport

plante-cu-balot-sau-in-container: What to choose for your project

For [street trees](/ghiduri/arbori-pentru-aliniamente-stradale), parks and tall [hedges](/gard-viu-en-gros) planted in autumn or spring, root-balled plants offer the best value. For projects with summer deadlines, for [perennials](/plante-perene-en-gros) and [shrubs](/arbusti-ornamentali-en-gros), containers are safer. Many projects combine both.

PlantDGD supplies both root-balled and container plants, depending on species and size. Send us your plant list, sizes and planting period via the [contact](/contact) page and we will recommend the right option.

plante-cu-balot-sau-in-container.q: How long can root-balled plants stay unplanted?
plante-cu-balot-sau-in-container.a: As briefly as possible – ideally they are planted within a few days of delivery. Until then they are kept in the shade with the root balls watered regularly.

plante-cu-balot-sau-in-container.q: Should the hessian be removed from the root ball at planting?
plante-cu-balot-sau-in-container.a: Natural hessian can be left in the hole, opened at the top. Wire or synthetic netting should be cut and partly removed.

plante-rezistente-la-seceta-spatii-verzi: Increasingly hot, dry summers and limited maintenance budgets make drought tolerance an essential criterion for public green spaces: roundabouts, squares, car parks, street plantings and slopes. Choosing the right species reduces water use, the number of interventions and plant losses.
Choose species adapted to full sun and poor, well-drained soils.
Group plants by water needs so irrigation is efficient.
Use mulch (bark or gravel) to reduce evaporation and weeds.
Plant in autumn so the roots develop before the first summer.
Ensure watering in the first 1–2 years – even drought-tolerant plants need water until they are established.

[Black pine](/products/pin-negru-pinus-nigra) is one of the most drought-, wind- and lime-tolerant trees, suited to parks and shelterbelts. [Creeping juniper](/products/ienupar-tarator-juniperus-horizontalis) covers slopes and roundabouts with a green carpet that needs almost no maintenance. [Oriental thuja](/products/tuia-orientala-platycladus-orientalis) is the choice for hedges in hot regions. See all [wholesale conifers](/conifere-en-gros).

Ornamental grasses are the stars of modern low-maintenance schemes. [Fountain grass (Pennisetum)](/products/pennisetum-alopecuroides) forms decorative clumps from summer to winter and needs only one cut a year. [Festuca glauca](/products/festuca-glauca) has blue leaves and prefers poor, dry soils.
Drought-tolerant perennials bring flowers and colour with minimal water use:
[Daylily (Hemerocallis)](/products/crin-de-zi-hemerocallis) – extremely tough, suited to slopes and roadsides.
[Sedum spectabile](/products/sedum-spectabile) – pink flowers in late summer, a nectar plant.
[Sedum 'Angelina'](/products/sedum-angelina) – a golden carpet for sunny areas and green roofs.
[Lamb's ear](/products/stachys-byzantina) – silver leaves, ground cover in full sun.
[Gaura](/products/gaura-lindheimeri) – flowers from June to autumn, deep roots.
[Bearded iris (Iris germanica)](/products/stanjenel-iris-germanica) – drought tolerant, flowers in late spring.

A simple, effective scheme: a carpet of creeping juniper or sedum as the base, groups of Pennisetum for volume and movement, accents of Gaura and Sedum spectabile for summer and autumn flowers, all on a layer of mulch. The result is decorative all year and only needs a spring clean-up and one cut of the grasses.

plante-rezistente-la-seceta-spatii-verzi.a: No plant is completely watering-free in its first year. Once established, creeping juniper, black pine, sedum, Festuca glauca and Gaura withstand long periods without watering.
Creeping juniper, sedum, ornamental grasses such as Pennisetum, and tough perennials such as daylily and Gaura.

arbori-pentru-aliniamente-stradale: Street trees live in harsh conditions: compacted soil, limited root space, heat reflected from asphalt, pollution and de-icing salt. Choosing the right species and size is decisive for the planting to last for decades without causing problems with utilities, pavements or façades.
What to check before choosing the species
Street width and distance to buildings – these determine the maximum crown size.
Overhead and underground utilities – under power lines choose small species or globe-shaped forms.
The soil volume available for roots.
Maintenance requirements – large leaves, fruit or flowers falling on the pavement.

[Catalpa (Catalpa bignonioides)](/products/catalpa-bignonioides) is a classic shade tree for boulevards and parks: a broad crown, large leaves, white flowers in June–July and good tolerance of urban conditions. Globe-shaped forms are used for narrow streets.
[Japanese cherry (Prunus serrulata)](/products/cires-japonez-prunus-serrulata) is ideal for residential streets, squares and school yards: medium size, 6–8 m, and spectacular flowering in April.

[Black pine](/products/pin-negru-pinus-nigra) suits parks, roadsides and shelterbelts thanks to its drought and wind tolerance. For vertical accents along avenues and at entrances in regions with mild winters, [Italian cypress](/products/chiparos-italian-cupressus-sempervirens) creates striking rows.

In public spaces, trees with a trunk girth of 12–14 cm or more and a clear stem up to 2–2.5 m are usually planted, so they do not obstruct pedestrians and traffic. Large trees are supplied root-balled and planted in autumn or spring. More on formats in [Balled or container plants](/ghiduri/plante-cu-balot-sau-in-container).
Planting and care in the first years
Planting pits as large as possible, with good-quality soil and protection against compaction.
Anchoring with 2–3 stakes and trunk protection.
Regular watering in the first 2–3 years, including with irrigation bags.
Formative pruning to raise the crown and correct crossing branches.

arbori-pentru-aliniamente-stradale.q: Which trees are suitable under power lines?
arbori-pentru-aliniamente-stradale.a: Small species or globe-shaped forms that do not reach the wires; Japanese cherry and globe-shaped catalpa are often used.

arbori-pentru-aliniamente-stradale.q: How far apart are avenue trees planted?
arbori-pentru-aliniamente-stradale.a: It depends on the mature crown size: usually 6–8 m for medium trees and 8–10 m for large trees such as catalpa.

plante-pentru-acoperisuri-verzi: Extensive green roofs have a thin layer of substrate (usually 6–15 cm), are not watered or watered very rarely, and are exposed to sun, wind, heat and frost. Only a few groups of plants survive these conditions, and sedum species are the basis of almost every extensive green roof.
It stores water in its fleshy leaves and survives weeks without rain.
It has shallow roots, suited to thin substrates.
It tolerates strong sun, wind and frost.
It forms a dense carpet that protects the substrate from erosion.
It needs no mowing and very little maintenance.

[Sedum 'Angelina'](/products/sedum-angelina) has golden leaves that turn orange in winter and is one of the most used species for green roofs. [Sedum hybridum](/products/sedum-hybridum) forms a dense green carpet with yellow flowers and is extremely frost-hardy. [Sedum rupestre 'Blue'](/products/sedum-rupestre-blue) adds blue-grey tones, and [Sedum 'Watson'](/products/sedum-watson) pink-green rosettes. Combined in bands or patches of different colours, these species create decorative patterns visible from above.
On slightly deeper substrates you can add [Festuca glauca](/products/festuca-glauca) for texture and [Iberis sempervirens](/products/iberis-sempervirens) for white spring flowers.
